security_cat_code_injection_why: Untrusted input can reach a code or template evaluation path, allowing arbitrary code execution in your runtime.
security_cat_prototype_pollution_why: Lets an attacker inject properties onto Object.prototype. Downstream code that reads those keys can be tricked into privilege escalation, logic corruption, or denial of service.
security_cat_ssrf_why: A crafted request can coerce the server into calling internal addresses — reaching cloud-metadata endpoints or internal services that should never be exposed.
security_cat_credential_leak_why: Authorization headers or secrets can be forwarded to an unintended origin during redirect handling, exposing them to third parties.
security_cat_header_injection_why: Unsanitized values written into request headers can poison downstream requests or exfiltrate data.
security_cat_csrf_why: A forged cross-origin request can perform state-changing actions on behalf of an authenticated user.
security_cat_redos_why: A malicious input string triggers catastrophic regex backtracking, pinning a CPU core and stalling the event loop for every request.
security_cat_dos_why: Unbounded resource consumption lets an attacker exhaust memory or CPU and take the service offline.
security_cat_null_byte_why: A null byte can truncate URL parsing, letting input slip past validation and reach unintended targets.
security_cat_other_why: A known security weakness in this dependency version.

surface_step_create_a_function: Everything starts as a function. It receives its data without knowing whether that arrived as a path param, a query string, a message body or a queue job, so nothing you write here has to be rewritten when the transport changes.
surface_step_enhance_it: Give it the things a function needs to be worth calling: typed errors it can throw, configuration it can read, and secrets and credentials it never has to hold itself.
surface_step_wire_it_up: Now decide how the outside world reaches it. Each wiring is one call, and a function can carry several — the same handler answering an HTTP route, a queue job and an MCP tool.
surface_step_guard_it: Say who may call it. Sessions come from auth, scopes gate the call outside the permission pool, and neither lives inside the function body.
surface_step_orchestrate_it: Compose functions into something longer-running: a workflow with durable steps and retries, or an agent that chooses which of them to call.
surface_step_test_it: Drive the whole thing the way a user would, in scenarios that run against a real server rather than a mocked one.

help_functions_what: A function is one piece of your app's logic — “create a booking”, “send the welcome email”. You write it once, and it knows nothing about how it was called.
help_functions_behaviour: Every function your project defines is on [this list](#list), whether it is reached over HTTP, from a queue, on a schedule, or by another function. Use [the search box](#search) to find one by name, then [pick it](#list) to see what it takes in, what it gives back, and which wirings call it.
help_functions_surprise: Functions are read from your code, not registered here — this screen is a view of what you have written, so nothing on it can be added or edited from the console. Pikku's own internal functions are hidden by default; [show them](#internals) only when you are debugging the framework itself.
help_functions_do_select: [Open one to see its inputs, outputs and wirings](#list)
help_flags_what: A feature flag is a switch around a piece of your app, so the code can ship before the feature is meant to be seen. This board shows every flag your code declares, sorted into the lane its launch has actually reached.
help_flags_behaviour: A flag moves left to right: **Dark** is off for everyone, **Rolling out** admits a share of subjects by bucket — the same subject stays in or out across requests — and **Live** is on for everyone the capabilities allow. [Open a flag](#board) to switch it, set its rollout share, or pin a named organization or user on or off regardless of the share.
help_flags_surprise: A flag declared in code with no row in the store **fails open**: it resolves on, for everybody, and it reports itself exactly like a flag you deliberately launched. That is what the [Needs attention](#board) lane is for — it is checked before every other reading, so a flag that is live by accident never sits quietly under Live. [Create missing rows](#flags-sync) gives those flags a row; [Prune undeclared](#flags-prune) removes rows whose declaration has gone from the code.
help_flags_do_open: [Open a flag to switch it or set its rollout](#board)
help_flags_do_override: [Pin one organization or user on or off](#board)
help_flags_do_sync: [Create store rows for flags that have none](#flags-sync)
help_analytics_what: An analytics event is a thing your app reports that happened — “page viewed”, “checkout completed” — together with the props that describe it. This screen is the catalog of every event your code declares, grouped by the file that declares it.
help_analytics_behaviour: Each event shows its props as the schema text your declaration wrote, so the card reads as the call that emits it. [Open one](#catalog) for the full prop list and the file it is declared in, or [search](#search) by event name or prop name.
help_analytics_surprise: This is what a client **may** emit, not what anything **has** emitted — there are no counts here, and no volume to read. It comes from build-time meta, so an event you just declared appears after the next `pikku` run, and one you deleted disappears at the same time.
help_analytics_do_open: [Open an event to see every prop and its schema](#catalog)
help_analytics_do_search: [Find an event by its name or a prop name](#search)

help_virtual_users_what: A virtual user is an AI stand-in for one kind of person who uses your app — a guest booking a seminar, an admin working through enquiries. It signs in as that person and uses the app to reach their goals.
help_virtual_users_behaviour: Pick someone in [the list](#list) to see who they are, how they behave and what they’ll try to do. [Send them on a visit](#try) and the report shows up under [Visits](#visits).
help_virtual_users_surprise: A try that finds nothing does not prove there are no problems — only that this visit didn’t hit one. Every try uses AI credit, and a virtual user never goes on your live site unless a developer allows it there.
help_virtual_users_examples: Examples: a guest in a hurry, a first-time visitor, an admin clearing enquiries.
virtual_users_found_server_error: {name} hit an error on your site
virtual_users_found_schema_violation: Your app gave {name} a broken answer

virtual_users_schedule_open: Let them visit on their own…
virtual_users_visiting_body: This usually takes a few minutes. You can leave this page; the report will be waiting under Visits.
virtual_users_fact_safe: Visits your preview site only. Your live site and real customers are never touched.
virtual_users_fact_time: A visit ends after 40 actions, or sooner if they finish what they came to do.
virtual_users_fact_cost: Each visit costs a little, which is why nothing runs until you ask.
virtual_users_flag_read_only: Only looks and never changes anything, even where they’re allowed to
virtual_users_flag_empty_memory: Arrives remembering nothing, every single visit
virtual_users_flag_inverted: Tries what they shouldn’t be allowed to. Getting through is the problem they report
virtual_users_tasks_note: Your team wrote these as step-by-step tests. {name} only gets the goal, never the steps, so they have to find their own way around, just like a real person would. If they can’t, that’s worth knowing.
virtual_users_reach_everything: Can use every part of your app: all {total} actions. {mutations} of them change data, like creating, editing and cancelling things.
virtual_users_reach_read_only: Can look at {offered} of your app’s {total} actions. Everything that would change data is switched off, because a checker only looks.
virtual_users_reach_some: Can use {offered} of your app’s {total} actions, the ones their role allows. The other {off} are off-limits to them.
virtual_users_reach_inverted: Is shown all {total} of your app’s actions on purpose, to check that their role really keeps them out.
virtual_users_role_line: Their permissions come from the {roles} role, the same one a real person in that role gets.
virtual_users_role_none: They have no role, so they only get what anyone signed in can use.
virtual_users_schedule_off_text: Off. {name} only visits when you send them. Turn this on and they’ll turn up at a random time, somewhere between every {min} and {max} hours, so nobody is watching when they find something.
virtual_users_schedule_on_text: On. {name} turns up at a random time, somewhere between every {min} and {max} hours. Next visit {when}.
virtual_users_no_visits: Send {name} on a visit and the report lands here: what they tried, what broke, and what confused them. If they find nothing, that’s good news for today, not a guarantee.
virtual_users_dev_sync: Provision the account and roles (additive, never revokes)
virtual_users_dev_schedule: Override what a scheduled visit does
virtual_users_report_all: {name} managed everything they came to do.
virtual_users_report_some: {name} managed {reached} of the {total} things they came to do.
virtual_users_report_none: {name} didn’t manage what they came to do.
virtual_users_report_problems_one: They ran into 1 problem on the way.
virtual_users_report_problems_other: They ran into {count} problems on the way.
virtual_users_steps_title: What they did, step by step
virtual_users_report_footer: A visit with no problems is good news for today, not a guarantee. Each visit goes a little differently.
virtual_users_empty_heading: Let AI stand-ins try your app before your users do
virtual_users_empty_body: A virtual user pretends to be one kind of person who uses your app: a busy admin, a first-time visitor, a customer in a hurry. They sign in to your preview site, try to get something done, and tell you in plain words where they got stuck or what broke.
virtual_users_benefit_people: Some are careful, some are distracted, some have never seen your app. Each finds different problems.
virtual_users_benefit_safe: They only visit your preview site, and only use what their role allows.
virtual_users_benefit_report: What they tried and what went wrong, in plain words. No logs to read.
virtual_users_empty_start: Describe the people who use your app to whoever builds it. Each one they add shows up here.
virtual_users_intro_title: Virtual users are AI stand-ins for the people who use your app.
virtual_users_intro_body: Each one pretends to be a real kind of user: an administrator, a guest filling in a form, an owner checking the books. You send them into your app, they try to get things done the way that person would, and they come back and tell you where they got stuck or something broke.
virtual_users_intro_meet: They’re built from the test stories your team already wrote. Pick one on the left to see who they are.
virtual_users_intro_send: They sign in to your preview site and use it on their own for a few minutes. Your live site is never touched.
virtual_users_intro_read: You get a short report in plain words: what they tried and what went wrong.
virtual_users_trait_sticks_explain: How often they finish what they start instead of wandering off or giving up.
virtual_users_trait_checks_explain: How often they look again instead of trusting what they remember.
virtual_users_trait_twice_explain: The impatient double-click. Catches duplicate bookings and double payments.
virtual_users_schedule_gap_hint: They pick a random moment in this window, so their visits are hard to predict.
virtual_users_goal_add: Add a goal and press Enter
virtual_users_goals_none: No goals. They’ll only do the tasks from your test stories.
users_page_description: Everyone who has signed up to your app.
users_people_blurb: Click someone to see what they can do. Use the menu to sign them out, reset their password or block them.
users_none_blurb: Nobody has signed up yet. When someone creates an account in your app, they show up here.
users_missing_title: Your app doesn't have user management yet
users_missing_blurb: Once your app includes it, everyone who signs up shows up here, and you can add people, sign them out or block them. Ask your developer to switch it on.
users_missing_dev_body: This deployment answered 404 for admin:listUsers, so the running build does not include @pikku/addon-admin's user functions. Check the app wires it (wireAddon name "admin") and redeploy.
users_load_failed_title: We couldn't load your app's users
users_load_failed_blurb: Your app didn't answer when we asked for its users. Try again in a moment.
scenarios_verdict_passed_body: Each scenario was acted out step by step, and your app did what every one of them describes.
scenarios_verdict_failed_body: Your app didn't do what some scenarios describe. Each one that failed is open below, with the step it stopped on and a recording of what happened.
scenarios_verdict_running_body: The scenarios are being acted out now. Each one fills in below as it finishes.
scenarios_skipped_blurb: These scenarios were held back from this run, each for the reason shown.
scenarios_untested_blurb: Changes people can make in the app that no scenario performs yet.
scenarios_untested_lines: {covered} of {total} functions fully reached in the last measured run
scenarios_dev_hint: Run it from the command line
personas_hero_body: Your scenarios act as these people, and virtual users sign in as them to try your app. The roles each one holds decide what they can see and do.
personas_people_blurb: Open someone to see their goals, what they can reach and the scenarios they appear in.
personas_systems_title: Things that act on their own
personas_systems_blurb: Your app and the services it connects to also do things in scenarios. Nobody signs in as them.
personas_systems_none: Nothing acts on its own here yet.
authproviders_page_description: The ways people can sign in to your app.
authproviders_hero_none_body: Switch on at least one way below so people can get into your app.
authproviders_hero_body: Adding another way is optional. Each one lets people use an account they already have, and only needs a few keys from the company that runs it.
authproviders_off_blurb: Pick one to see how to set it up. It takes a few minutes at the company that runs it.
authproviders_builtin: Built in, nothing to set up
authproviders_email_description: People sign up with their email address and a password.
authproviders_account_description: People sign in with their {name} account.
authproviders_dev_callback: Every provider sends people back to
authproviders_step_create_body: This is where {name} gives you the keys your app needs.
authproviders_step_return_title: Tell {name} where to send people back
authproviders_step_return_body: Paste this after your app’s address, where {name} asks for a redirect or callback URL.
authproviders_key_keep: Leave blank to keep the saved one
authproviders_save_failed: The keys couldn’t be saved. Try again.
authproviders_builtin_body: Email and password sign-in is part of your app already. There’s nothing to set up here.
authproviders_email_off_body: Your app doesn’t have email and password sign-in. A developer switches it on in the app’s code.
integrations_browse_blurb: Open any of them to see what it does and what you’ll need.
integrations_dev_body: Each integration is an npm package of functions and agents. Adding one installs the package into your project under a name you choose.
scopes_page_desc_plain: Everything people can be allowed to do in your app, and which roles allow it.
scopes_hero_blurb: Each line below is something a person can be allowed to do in your app. Your developers define them in code; you give them to people by giving them a role.
scopes_given_to_nobody: Not part of any role yet
scopes_dev_prune: Run pikku scopes prune to remove scopes that are no longer declared.
scopes_empty_blurb: Your app doesn't define any permissions yet. A developer adds them in code.
scopes_forbidden_blurb: Ask someone who manages your team to give you access to permissions.
scopes_load_failed_blurb: Something went wrong reaching your app. Try again in a moment.
scopes_no_match_blurb: Try a different word, or clear the search to see everything.
scopes_roles_unavailable: Roles couldn't be loaded, so who holds each permission isn't shown.
scopes_source_app_blurb: Defined in your app's own code.
scopes_source_generated_title: Added to your app by Pikku
scopes_source_generated_blurb: Pikku generated these into your project, from your personas or a feature you scaffolded.
scopes_source_removed_blurb: Nothing declares these any more. They grant nothing and can be pruned.
scopes_no_match_filters_blurb: Clear a filter to see more.
roles_page_desc_plain: Named sets of permissions you give to people.
roles_hero_blurb: A role is a named set of permissions. Give someone a role and they can do everything it allows; change the role and everyone who holds it changes with it.
roles_list_blurb: Open a role to choose what it allows. You give roles to people on the Users page.
roles_list_empty_blurb: There are no roles yet. Create one, choose what it allows, then give it to people on the Users page.
roles_forbidden_blurb: Ask someone who manages your team to give you access to permissions.
roles_load_failed_blurb: Something went wrong reaching your app. Try again in a moment.
roles_editor_new_body: Name the role, say who it is for, then tick what it allows.
roles_editor_edit_body: Tick what this role allows. Everyone who holds it gets the change straight away.
webhooks_list_blurb: Each one is a message your app sends to another service. Open one to see what it carries and where it went.
webhooks_empty: Your app hasn't sent any webhooks yet. They'll show up here the first time one goes out.
webhooks_dev_signing: Every body is signed with HMAC in the X-Pikku-Signature header, unless config.webhook.signatureHeader names another. Failed sends are retried by the queue.
webhooks_carries_unknown: What it carries isn't described yet.
webhooks_goes_to_none: It hasn't gone anywhere yet. Each address it's sent to will show here.
webhooks_none_declared: Your app doesn't list its webhooks yet. What it has sent is below.
webhooks_other_blurb: Messages your app sent that aren't in the list above.
webhooks_dev_declare: Declare an event with defineWebhook, giving it an event key, a title and a payload schema, so it's listed before it's first sent and webhookService.send checks its data.
integrations_description: Connect your app to the services you already use.
integrations_hero_title: Connect your app to services you already use
integrations_hero_blurb: Take payments, send emails, book meetings, use AI and more. Pick what you want your app to do, and each one shows you how to add it.
integrations_apis_hero_blurb: Thousands of online services let other apps talk to them. Find the one you need and bring it into your app.
integrations_popular_blurb: The services most apps start with.
integrations_next_check: Open it to check it’s set up and see what it can do.
integrations_next_keys: Next: open it and paste in your keys.
integrations_next_ready: Set up and working. Open it to see what it can do.
integrations_dev_body_apis: Each web service here publishes an OpenAPI description. Importing one generates a package of functions from it.
integrations_detail_dev_hint: Package, version and everything inside it
integrations_need_keys: Your keys from {name}. You paste them in after adding it.
integrations_need_maybe_account: An account with {name}, if it asks for one
integrations_need_nothing: Nothing else. It works as soon as it’s added.
integrations_step_name: Keep the suggested name below, or pick your own.
integrations_step_keys: Open its Setup tab and paste in your keys from {name}.
integrations_step_use: That’s it. Your app and its AI assistants can now use it.
integrations_name_hint: Only change this if you’re adding the same service twice.
integrations_job_hubspot: Keep track of customers in HubSpot
integrations_cat_monitoring: Keep an eye on your app
integrations_readonly_hint: This is your live app, so nothing can be added here. Open a sandbox to add it.
wires_cli_description: Commands someone can type in a terminal to use your app
wires_cli_blurb: Anyone with the {program} command-line tool can run these. Open a command to see how to run it.
wires_cli_no_commands: This program has no commands yet.
wires_cli_empty_description: When your app offers commands for a terminal, they show up here with how to run each one.
wires_mcp_description: Let AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor use your app
wires_mcp_connect_blurb: Give your AI assistant this address and it can use everything listed below. Pick the assistant you use and copy its setup.
wires_mcp_connect_dev_note: This is the default /mcp path on this stage. If the project sets its own mcpPath, or serves more than one MCP surface, use that path instead.
wires_mcp_client_claude_desktop_how: Add this to claude_desktop_config.json, or paste the address into Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector.
wires_mcp_client_claude_code_how: Run this once in a terminal.
wires_mcp_client_cursor_how: Add this to .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or to ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project.
wires_mcp_tools_blurb: Things an assistant can do in your app for you when you ask it to.
wires_mcp_resources_blurb: Information from your app an assistant can look at to answer questions.
wires_mcp_prompts_blurb: Instructions your app hands the assistant so people can start common jobs in one step.
wires_mcp_row_no_description_hint: The assistant only sees this name. Adding a description helps it choose this at the right moment.
wires_mcp_empty_description: Your app doesn't offer anything to AI assistants yet. A developer can add MCP tools, resources or prompts.
wires_channels_description: Live connections that keep your app's screens up to date the moment something changes
wires_channels_empty_description: A channel keeps a screen connected to your app so it updates instantly, without anyone refreshing. Use one for things like a live booking list, chat, or notifications. They appear here once your app defines one.
wires_channels_blurb: A screen opens this connection once and stays connected. Your app can then push updates to it instantly, and the screen can send the messages below.
wires_channels_access_public: Anyone who has the address. No sign-in is needed, so only send what is safe to share.
wires_channels_access_signed_in: Only people signed in to your app. Everyone else is turned away.
wires_channels_connect_meta: Your app runs a step as soon as a screen opens this connection
wires_channels_disconnect_meta: Your app tidies up when a screen closes or loses its connection
wires_channels_message_meta: Messages that don't ask for a specific action are handled here
wires_channels_action_meta: A screen sends “{action}” to ask for this
wires_channels_dev_hint: Path, routing keys and a connect snippet
credentials_page_description: The services your app signs in to
credentials_hero_title_one: Your app signs in to 1 service
credentials_hero_title: Your app signs in to {count} services
credentials_hero_body: Credentials let your app sign in to other companies’ services on your behalf.
credentials_hero_body_missing: Credentials let your app sign in to other companies’ services on your behalf. Until a service is connected, the parts of your app that use it won’t work.
credentials_services_title: Services your app signs in to
credentials_services_blurb_app: Connect once and every part of your app can use it.
credentials_services_blurb_me: Services you connect with your own account, for your own use.
credentials_services_blurb_customers: Each customer connects these with their own account. Open one to see what they’ve connected.
credentials_none_app: Nothing is shared by the whole app.
credentials_none_me: There’s nothing for you to connect with your own account.
credentials_none_customers: No service asks each customer to connect their own.
credentials_no_customers: No customer has connected anything yet.
credentials_dev_hint: Keys, sign-in type and where each is declared
agents_page_description: AI assistants that talk to people and act for them
agents_hero_title_one: 1 AI assistant works in your app
agents_hero_title: {count} AI assistants work in your app
agents_hero_body: Each one talks to people in plain language and can take actions for them — like finding a product or placing an order. Open one to chat with it and see what it can do.
agents_list_blurb: What each one is for and what it’s allowed to do.
scorers_page_description: Checks that grade your assistants’ answers
scorers_hero_idle_title: Your assistants’ answers aren’t being graded
scorers_hero_body: Quality checks read what your assistants say and score it, so you can see when answers get worse.
scorers_hero_body_idle_one: Quality checks read what your assistants say and score it, so you can see when answers get worse. You have 1 check, but it isn’t attached to an assistant yet.
scorers_hero_body_idle: Quality checks read what your assistants say and score it, so you can see when answers get worse. You have {count} checks, but none is attached to an assistant yet.
scorers_list_blurb: Each check asks one question about an answer. Quick checks are rules in your code; thorough ones ask an AI model to judge.
scorers_tests_only: only in tests with an answer key
scorers_dev_hint: Code names, lanes and sampling rates
workflows_page_description: Workflows your app runs by itself, step by step
workflows_hero_body: A workflow is a series of steps your app runs by itself, even when they take hours.
workflows_hero_body_never: A workflow is a series of steps your app runs by itself, even when they take hours. None of them has run here yet.
workflows_list_blurb: Open one to see its steps and every time it has run.
workflows_status_compensation_failed: Last run rolled back — some steps are stuck
workflows_dev_hint: Code names, step counts and step functions
gateway_page_description: Where messages from chat platforms come into your app
gateway_page_hero_title_one: Your app answers messages from 1 place
gateway_page_hero_title: Your app answers messages from {count} places
gateway_page_hero_body: A gateway connects a messaging platform, like Slack, WhatsApp or a chat box on your site, to your app. Each message someone sends is passed to your app, and its reply goes back the same way.
gateway_page_list_blurb: Open one to see who can use it and what answers its messages.
gateway_page_meta_websocket: People chat from a screen that connects to {route}
gateway_page_meta_webhook: A platform sends each message to {route}
gateway_page_meta_listener: Your app listens for messages itself, so there is no address
gateway_page_dev_hint: Names, addresses and the function each one calls
scheduler_page_description: Tasks your app runs by itself at set times
scheduler_page_hero_title_one: Your app runs 1 task on a schedule
scheduler_page_hero_title: Your app runs {count} tasks on a schedule
scheduler_page_hero_body: Each task starts by itself at the times below, with nobody pressing anything. Times follow your deployment's timezone.
scheduler_page_list_blurb: Open one to see what it runs and exactly when.
scheduler_page_dev_hint: Code names, functions and cron expressions
trigger_page_description: Starts work in your app when something happens elsewhere
trigger_page_empty_description: A trigger starts a step in your app when something happens somewhere else. Once your app declares one, it shows up here.
trigger_page_hero_body: A trigger listens for something that happens outside your app, and each time it does, runs a step in your app.
trigger_page_list_blurb: Open one to see what it listens to and the step it runs.
trigger_page_dev_hint: Code names and the functions each trigger wires together
webhook_source_intro: {source} sends a message to your app each time something happens there. Your app receives it at the address below and hands each event to the trigger listening for it.
webhook_source_events_none: It doesn't list the events it sends.
webhook_source_steps: What it does on its own
webhook_source_step_receive: Reads and checks each message before passing it on
webhook_source_step_check: Checks the connection is still in place
webhook_source_step_setup: Connects itself to {source} when you turn it on
webhook_source_step_teardown: Disconnects itself from {source} when you turn it off
webhook_source_secret_stored: Saved. Each message is checked to prove it really came from {source}.
webhook_source_secret_missing: Not saved yet. Until it is, your app can't prove messages really came from {source}.
queue_page_description: Jobs your app does in the background, so nobody waits for them
queue_page_hero_body: A queue holds jobs your app does after it has answered, like sending an email, so nobody has to wait for them. Each queue has one function that works through its jobs.
queue_page_yours_blurb: Written for this app. Open one to see the function that does the work.
queue_page_system_blurb: Come with the platform for its built-in features. You don't need to change them.
queue_page_workflow_meta: Moves this workflow from one step to the next
queue_page_empty_description: When your app has work to do in the background, its queues show up here.
queue_page_dev_hint: Queue names, the functions that do the work and their settings
runtime_page_description: What your app is built on: shared services, middleware and permissions
runtime_page_hero_body: Services are the shared tools every part of your app uses, like the database and email. Middleware runs before a request reaches your app, and permissions decide who may call what.
runtime_page_services_blurb: The shared tools your app's functions use. The most used come first.
runtime_page_middleware_blurb: Steps that run before a request reaches your app's functions. Open one to see where it applies.
runtime_page_permissions_blurb: Rules that decide who may call a function. Open one to see what it protects.
runtime_page_dev_hint_services: Code names and the functions that use each
runtime_page_dev_hint_rules: Code names, exports and where each applies
runtime_page_services_yours_blurb: Written for this app. The most used come first.
runtime_page_services_builtin_blurb: Come with pikku and Fabric, so your app doesn't have to build them. The most used come first.
runtime_page_middleware_yours_blurb: Written for this app. Each runs before a request reaches your functions. Open one to see where it applies.
runtime_page_middleware_builtin_blurb: Comes with pikku and Fabric. Each runs before a request reaches your functions. Open one to see where it applies.
runtime_page_permissions_yours_blurb: Written for this app. Each decides who may call a function. Open one to see what it protects.
runtime_page_permissions_builtin_blurb: Come with pikku and Fabric. Each decides who may call a function. Open one to see what it protects.
scheduler_status_no_runs: No runs in the last week
webhook_source_registration_pending: {source} can be turned on after the next publish.
webhook_source_registration_registered: {source} knows where to send its events.
webhook_source_registration_manual: {source} can't be set up automatically. Follow the steps below once.
webhook_source_registration_failed: Connecting {source} failed. Turn it off and on again to retry.
webhook_source_registration_off: {source} is off. Turn it on to connect it and start receiving its events.
webhook_source_orphan_body: {source} may still be sending events here. Remove the webhook in {source}, then confirm.
i18n_page_desc: The wording your app shows, in every language it speaks
i18n_none: No frontend in this workspace has translatable copy yet.
pages_empty_description: When your app has screens, each one shows up here with a picture of how it looks.
pages_failed_title: The screens could not be read
pages_failed_blurb: Something went wrong while looking for the screens of your app. Try again in a moment.
pages_hero_blurb_one: Your app has one screen. Take new pictures to see how it looks right now.
pages_hero_blurb: Your app has {count} screens. Take new pictures to see how each one looks right now.
pages_address_needed: Type the address your app is running at, then take new pictures.
pages_pictures_failed: The pictures could not be taken. Check that your app is running at this address.
pages_group_blurb: Pictures show what a visitor sees before signing in, so a screen that needs an account may show the sign-in screen instead.
pages_example_blurb: This screen shows one item at a time. Type an example so the picture has something to show.
pages_problems_one: We noticed one problem while opening this screen.
pages_problems: We noticed {count} problems while opening this screen.
pages_failed_open: This screen did not open, so there is no picture.
pages_dev_hint: Route files, paths and the CLI
pages_dev_routes: Screens are read from the TanStack Router file routes under each frontend's src/routes.
pages_dev_cli: Take the same pictures from a terminal and save them to disk
pages_dev_signed_out: Pictures are taken signed out at the browser's window size. The CLI can sign in as a persona first with --as; the console cannot yet.
pages_dev_not_saved: Pictures taken here are kept until the console reloads. The CLI saves its pictures under .pikku/pages/screenshots.
checks_never_title: Your app hasn't been checked yet
checks_never_description: A check looks through your app for mistakes that would stop pages or features from working. Run one to see how your app is doing.
checks_running_blurb: This usually takes under a minute. You can leave this page and come back.
checks_running_blurb_previous: This usually takes under a minute. Until it finishes, you're seeing the last check.
checks_healthy_blurb: Nothing in your app needs attention right now.
checks_attention_blurb_broken: Some parts of your app may not work until these are fixed.
checks_attention_blurb_minor: Your app works, but a few things could be better.
checks_failed_blurb: Something went wrong while running the check. Try again, or ask a developer to look at the details below.
checks_group_broken_blurb: These stop parts of your app from working properly.
checks_group_minor_blurb: Your app still works, but these could cause trouble later.
checks_group_info_blurb: Nothing is wrong, but a developer may want to know.
checks_steps_blurb: Each check looks at a different part of your app.
checks_step_checks_about: Looks for pages that can't open, data that's out of date and wording that can't be translated.
checks_step_codegen_about: Makes sure the app's building blocks are put together correctly.
checks_step_typecheck_about: Makes sure the code behind your app fits together.
checks_step_frontend_about: Makes sure the code behind the screens people use fits together.
checks_skipped_disabled: Not part of this check. A developer can include it by running the full check.
checks_skipped_codegen: Skipped because the app setup has a problem.
checks_skipped_catalog: Skipped because a translations file is damaged.
checks_skipped_not_installed: Skipped because the pikku tools aren't installed in this project.
checks_kind_orphan_about: A page is set up to show other pages inside it, but it never makes room for them, so they don't appear.
checks_kind_dataless_about: This page is meant to show one particular item, but it never loads that item.
checks_kind_wording_about: A piece of text on a screen is written straight into the code, so it stays in one language.
checks_kind_stale_title: The app is out of step with its database
checks_kind_stale_about: The database has changed since the app last read its layout, so some data isn't checked properly.
checks_kind_catalog_about: One of the files that holds your app's wording can't be read, so new wording shows up as missing.
checks_kind_timeout_about: Part of the check didn't finish in time, so we can't tell whether it's healthy.
checks_kind_server_title: A mistake in the server code
checks_kind_server_about: Part of the code behind your app doesn't fit with what it's connected to.
checks_kind_screens_title: A mistake in the screens' code
checks_kind_screens_about: Part of the code behind your app's screens doesn't fit with what it's connected to.
checks_kind_setup_title: A problem in the app setup
checks_kind_setup_about: Something in how the app is put together stops it from being prepared.
checks_kind_setup_minor_title: The app setup could be better
checks_kind_setup_minor_about: The app can still be prepared, but part of its setup is unusual or does nothing useful.
checks_kind_other_title: Something in your app looks wrong
checks_kind_other_about: A check found something that may not work as intended.
checks_todo_broken: Ask a developer to fix this. Everything they need is in the developer details below.
checks_todo_minor: Nothing is broken yet. Pass this on to a developer when there's time.
checks_dev_hint: Files, error codes and how to fix them
checks_dev_hint_run: Where the check ran and how to run every check yourself
checks_dev_run: Run every check, including the app setup
checks_dev_skips_codegen: Check again skips code generation because the dev server keeps it current. pikku verify runs everything, and its result shows up here too.
checks_dev_copy_all: All of it, to paste to a developer or an AI assistant
code_select_file_subtitle: Choose a file from the tree to view its contents.
config_secrets_hero_empty: Your app doesn't use any secrets yet
config_secrets_blurb: Passwords and keys your app needs to talk to other services. Values are stored encrypted and never shown in full.
config_variables_hero_empty: Your app doesn't read any settings yet
config_variables_blurb: Plain settings your app reads when it starts, like a web address or a limit. Unlike secrets, anyone with access can see them.
config_group_missing_blurb: Parts of your app that use these won't work until they're filled in.
config_group_optional_blurb: Your app works without these. Fill them in to switch on what they're for.
config_group_set_blurb: These have a value. Open one to change it.
config_group_unknown_blurb: Looking up whether these have a value.
security_hero_never_title: Your app hasn't been checked yet
security_hero_never_blurb: Your app is built on hundreds of packages other people wrote. Run a check to see if any of them have known weaknesses, and which ones have newer versions. Checking changes nothing.
security_what_blurb: It compares every package your app uses against public lists. Nothing is sent about your own code.
security_what_weak_about: Packages with a published security problem, how serious it is, and the version that fixes it.
security_what_outdated_about: Packages that have moved on, and whether updating is a small step or a big one.
security_dev_run: Run it from the command line
i18n_hero_blurb: Every button, heading and message your app shows, side by side with its translation. Pick a language to fill in what's missing; changes save as you leave each box.
i18n_base_about: The wording is written in this language first. Every other language translates from it.
i18n_languages_blurb: How far along each language is. Pick one to work on its wording.
i18n_wording_blurb: The {base} wording on the left, its {language} translation on the right. Red boxes still need a translation.
emails_samples_blurb: Each person gets their own name and links. Change these sample values to see how the email reads.
emails_samples_none: This email reads the same for everyone, so there's nothing to fill in.
config_secrets_hero_required_set: Every secret your app needs is set
config_variables_hero_required_set: Every setting your app needs is set
requests_description_local: What you want changed in this app
requests_description_fabric: What people asked to change on the live app
requests_new_blurb: Say what you want in plain words. The builder picks it up from here.
requests_empty_description_local: Write down what you want changed and the builder works through it, one at a time.
requests_empty_description_fabric: When someone asks for a change on the live app, it shows up here for you to pick up.
requests_hero_body_local: These live in the project folder, so they travel with your code.
requests_hero_body_fabric: This project is published, so requests come from the people using it. Finishing one tells them it's done.
requests_section_blocked_blurb: The builder has a question before it can carry on.
requests_section_waiting_blurb: In the order they were asked for.
help_requests_what: A to-do list for your app. Each request is one thing you, or someone using the app, wants changed.
help_requests_behaviour: Requests are worked through in the order they were asked for. One that needs an answer from you moves to the top and waits there.
help_requests_surprise: On a project that is only on your computer, requests are kept in the project folder. Once it is published they come from Fabric, from the people using the live app, and you can't add new ones here.
help_requests_examples: "Make the sign-up button bigger", "The prices page shows the wrong currency", "Add a dark mode".
help_requests_do_finish: Mark one done, dismiss it, or bring a finished one back
wishes_blurb: Ten things your app could let people do, smallest first. Like the ones you want and the builder keeps them in mind.
wishes_no_model: Sign in with Fabric, or add an AI key, to get ideas for where your app could go.
studio_welcome_blurb: Build apps on your own computer. Choose how you want to work — you can change this later.
studio_local_blurb: Everything stays here. No account needed. You can sign in with Fabric later to put an app online.
studio_fabric_choice_blurb: See the apps you already have on Fabric, use its AI models, and publish with one button.
studio_fabric_blurb: Fabric will ask you to confirm this code. It keeps your password out of Studio.
studio_fabric_steps: Open Fabric, check the code matches this one, and confirm.
studio_fabric_expired: The code ran out before it was confirmed.
studio_fabric_rejected: The sign-in was turned down in Fabric.
studio_fabric_unreachable: Studio could not reach Fabric. Check your connection and try again.
studio_projects_blurb_local: The apps you are building on this computer. Open one to work on it.
studio_projects_blurb_fabric: The apps on this computer and the ones in your Fabric account. Open one to work on it.
studio_new_blurb: Give it a name and say what it is for. Studio sets it up and suggests where it could go while it gets ready.
studio_new_idea_hint: A sentence or two is enough, like “A log of when I water my plants”.
studio_add_title: Add a project you already have
studio_add_blurb: Point Studio at the folder the app lives in. Nothing in the folder is moved.
studio_local_section_blurb: Studio works on a copy of each one, so your own folder is never changed behind your back.
studio_local_section_empty: Nothing here yet. Start a new project, or add a folder you already have.
studio_cloud_section_blurb: These apps are online but not on this computer. Copy one here to work on it.
studio_cloud_section_empty: Every app in your Fabric account is already on this computer.
studio_cloud_no_repo: Fabric has no code for this app to copy yet.
studio_account_local: You are working on this computer only.
studio_account_fabric: You are signed in to Fabric at {url}.
wishes_subscription: Ideas need an API key or Fabric. Your subscription is used for building, not for ideas.
studio_ai_blurb: Studio uses an AI to build your app with you. Pick how it gets one — you can change this any time.
studio_ai_key_blurb: Bring a key from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and others. You pay that company for what you use.
studio_ai_key_form_blurb: The key stays on this computer. Studio gives it only to your projects while they run.
studio_ai_key_model_hint: Leave empty for a fast, low-cost one.
studio_ai_sub_title: Use a subscription you already pay for
studio_ai_sub_blurb: Sign in with ChatGPT Plus or Pro, Grok or GitHub Copilot. It uses your plan's allowance, which can run out on a long build.
studio_ai_sub_form_blurb: The builder signs in to your subscription itself. Studio never sees your password or your plan's tokens.
studio_ai_sub_steps: In a terminal, start the builder and sign in:
studio_ai_sub_claude_note: Claude Pro and Max are not offered: Anthropic bills their use outside its own apps per token, not from your plan. Add an Anthropic API key instead.
studio_ai_fabric_blurb: Sign in with Fabric for many models in one place, including low-cost ones. No keys to manage.
studio_ai_fabric_blurb_signed_in: You are signed in to Fabric, so it can provide many models, including low-cost ones. No keys to manage.
studio_publish_blurb: Put your app on the internet so other people can use it. Pick where it should live — you can publish to more than one place.
studio_publish_fabric_blurb: Fabric runs your app for you: it builds it, gives it an address and keeps it running. Publishing saves your latest work and sends it to Fabric.
studio_publish_fabric_sign_in: Fabric runs your app for you: it builds it, gives it an address and keeps it running. Sign in with Fabric from All projects to use it.
studio_publish_fabric_not_in_fabric: This project is only on your computer. Add it to Fabric in the Fabric console first, then publish from here.
studio_publish_prompt_hint: Fabric publishes in one step. For anywhere else, copy the steps and paste them into your AI builder: it adds what your app needs for that place and asks you for any accounts or passwords on the way.
studio_publish_standalone_blurb: Turns your app into one file you can run on any computer or server with Node. You look after the server yourself.
studio_publish_cloudflare_blurb: Runs your app on Cloudflare's network, close to the people using it. You need a Cloudflare account.
studio_publish_serverless_blurb: Runs your app on AWS Lambda, which only charges while it is in use. You need an AWS account.
studio_publish_azure_blurb: Runs your app as Azure Functions. Useful if your company already uses Microsoft's cloud. You need an Azure account.
help_publish_what: Where you put your app on the internet so other people can use it.
help_publish_behaviour: Fabric publishes in one step. Every other place gives you a set of steps to hand to your AI builder, which sets the project up for that place.
help_publish_surprise: Publishing with Fabric saves your latest work first, so everything you have changed goes live together.
help_publish_examples: Share the app with your team on Fabric, run it on a server you already have, or put it on Cloudflare.
help_publish_do_fabric: Publish with Fabric in one step
help_publish_do_copy: Copy the steps for another place and paste them into your AI builder
studio_db_outdated: This project's database is behind the version of Pikku it uses. Studio can add the missing tables and start it again.
studio_builder_placeholder: Describe what you want to build or change
studio_builder_follow_up: Add to what the builder is doing
studio_builder_empty_title: Tell the builder what to make
studio_builder_empty_body: It works on a copy of this project, so your own files stay as they are until you keep the changes.
weaving_empty_subtitle: As the builder writes functions, routes and screens, they'll appear here.
design_panel_click_hint: Click any element in the preview to inspect its design properties.
design_panel_component_empty: Click an element in the preview to edit that component's theme defaults.
design_panel_component_hint: Defaults for every {component} in the app. Element props override these.
design_panel_component_no_props: This component has no themable defaults.
design_panel_no_props: No design props available for this element.
design_panel_prop_align_desc: How children line up on the cross axis
design_panel_prop_bd_desc: Border shorthand — width, style, and color
design_panel_prop_bottom_desc: Distance from the bottom edge (when positioned)
design_panel_prop_color_desc: Theme color applied to this component
design_panel_prop_display_desc: How this element participates in layout
design_panel_prop_inset_desc: Shorthand for top, right, bottom, left
design_panel_prop_justify_desc: How children are spread along the main axis
design_panel_prop_left_desc: Distance from the left edge (when positioned)
design_panel_prop_mx_desc: Outer space on the horizontal sides
design_panel_prop_my_desc: Outer space on the vertical sides
design_panel_prop_offset_desc: Empty columns left before this element
design_panel_prop_pos_desc: How this element sits in the document flow
design_panel_prop_px_desc: Inner space on the horizontal sides
design_panel_prop_py_desc: Inner space on the vertical sides
design_panel_prop_right_desc: Distance from the right edge (when positioned)
design_panel_prop_span_desc: How many grid columns this takes up
design_panel_prop_top_desc: Distance from the top edge (when positioned)
design_panel_prop_variant_desc: Visual style preset for this component
design_panel_prop_wrap_desc: Let children wrap onto the next line
design_panel_theme_auto_contrast_desc: Flip text color automatically for readable contrast on filled components
design_panel_theme_empty: This app has no editable theme.
design_panel_theme_font_body_desc: Font family used for body text
design_panel_theme_hint: Edits change the active theme — they apply everywhere in the app.
design_panel_theme_primary_desc: The main accent color used by every component
design_panel_theme_role_desc: Base color for this role — components using it update everywhere
design_panel_theme_scheme_desc: The scheme the app boots with
design_panel_theme_shade_desc: Which shade (0–9) of the primary scale filled components use
studio_apps_failed: The {slug} app did not start. Its log is in Studio's logs folder.
builder_no_preview_subtitle: This project does not expose a frontend right now. Use Chat to create one, or open the Code tab to inspect the workspace.
studio_check_verify: The code doesn't check out yet
studio_check_plan: Parts of the plan aren't built yet
studio_milestone_should_do_blurb: The scenario the builder runs to prove this milestone works.
studio_milestone_plan_blurb: What the builder promised to build for this milestone. Greyed items come in a later pass.
studio_milestone_no_plan: The builder writes a plan before it starts building.
studio_milestone_not_checked: Not checked yet. The builder checks the milestone each time it finishes a turn.
studio_milestone_pages_blurb: Each page photographed on a computer and a phone, and graded on how it looks.
studio_milestones_empty_body: Tell the builder what you want in the chat. It writes your app down as milestones, then builds them one at a time.
studio_milestones_blurb: Your app, in the order the builder builds it. Open one to see its plan, its last check and its pages.
studio_keep_waiting: Changes made here aren't in your {folder} folder yet. Until you keep them, the builder works on its own copy.
studio_keep_nothing: Your {folder} folder has everything made here.
studio_keep_done: Done. Your {folder} folder now has these changes.
studio_keep_conflict: You changed the same lines in {folder} that the builder changed here, so nothing was moved. Ask the builder to work from your version of these files, then try again:
studio_keep_edited: These files have unsaved edits in {folder}, so nothing was moved. Save or undo them there, then try again:
studio_logs_empty: Nothing here yet. Your app's messages show up once it is running.
